q: You are on the ARC route, the GPS has failed and you want a noon latitude. At what UT is the Sun on your meridian?
why: Mer Pass 1148 LMT + 35°20′ of west longitude in time (2h21m) = 1409 UT; longitude west is added.

q: On passage from Cocos Keeling to Mauritius you plan the noon sight. At what UT do you expect the Sun on your meridian?
why: Mer Pass 1205 LMT − 72°45′ of east longitude in time (4h51m) = 0714 UT; longitude east is subtracted.

q: Your ship's clock keeps zone time +3 and you want to call the navigator on deck for noon. What will the ship's clock show at meridian passage?
why: 1153 + 3h09m for 47°10′W = 1502 UT; zone +3 means ship's time = UT − 3 h = 1202.

q: You are running west in the trades and want the UT of noon, allowing for your run. When will the Sun be on your meridian?
why: First guess 1149 + 2h40m = 1429; 4.5 h at 7 kn = 31 M = 33′ of longitude W → 40°33′W → 1149 + 2h42m = 1431 UT.

q: Your noon is predicted for 1409 UT. How do you take the meridian altitude?
a: Start ten minutes early and follow the Sun up until it stops rising
o: Take one sight at exactly 1409 UT, timed to the second
Start at 1409 UT and average the sights of the next ten minutes
Take sights from 1400 to 1420 UT and use the last one
why: Before noon the Sun climbs ever more slowly: keep it on the horizon until it stops rising — that highest altitude is the meridian altitude.

fig.title: Noon sight
lines: Watch checked against UT this morning

q: You follow the Sun up to noon and note these sextant readings. Which Hs do you reduce for your latitude?
why: The meridian altitude is the maximum: 50°46.4′ at 1410. A mean of readings either side of noon always comes out low.

q: Cloud covers the Sun through your predicted noon. At 1427 UT it comes out and you take a sight. What do you do with it?
a: Reduce it as an ordinary sun sight for a position line
o: Use it as the meridian altitude — the top is flat
Add 18′ to it, a minute of arc for each minute late
Discard it — after noon a sight gives nothing
why: 18 minutes after noon the Sun has dropped some 15′: work it with LHA, Hc and an intercept as a normal sun line.

q: Your noon sight on the ARC route gives this. Which working gives your latitude?
why: Sun south of you: Lat = Dec + z. With Dec south (−21°22.1′): −21°22.1′ + 38°59.1′ = 17°37.0′N.

q: Halfway from Bermuda to the Azores you take the noon sight on the longest day. What is your latitude?
Bound for Hawaii in July, you find the noon Sun bearing north of you. What is your latitude?
On the Puddle Jump, well out from the Galápagos, you take the noon sight. Where are you?
Sailing from St Helena to Ascension just before Christmas, you see the noon Sun south of you. What is your latitude?
Two days out of Cape Town for St Helena, the noon Sun bears north. What latitude do you plot?
Crossing the Bay of Bengal from Phuket to Sri Lanka in the NE monsoon, you take this noon sight but forget to note the Sun's bearing. What is your latitude?
why: Dec is south and you are north of the equator, so the Sun bears south: Lat = Dec + z = −21°09.2′ + 28°17.5′ = 7°08.3′N.

q: Your noon on the ARC route falls at 1409 UT. Which Dec do you use?
why: Dec changes 0.4′ an hour and is increasing: for 9 minutes add 0.4′ × 9/60 = 0.06′, so S21°22.0′ becomes S21°22.1′.

q: You are three minutes late for noon and take the sight anyway, treating it as the meridian altitude. How much lower than the true maximum is it?
a: About 0.4′ — the top of the curve is flat
o: About 4.4′ — over a minute of arc per minute
About 45′ — 15′ of arc per minute of time
About 1.3′ — it falls as fast as it rose
why: Near noon the altitude changes as the square of the time from noon: three minutes off costs only about 0.4′ here.

lines: Noon (LAN) 1409 UT, you sight at 1412 UT

fig.title: Evening twilight, 20 Jun 2026
lines: Arcturus on the meridian, bearing south

q: North of the Caribbean at evening twilight, you catch Capella on your meridian, bearing north. What is your latitude?

fig.title: Evening twilight, 1 Mar 2027
lines: Capella on the meridian, bearing north

q: Bound for the Azores in early May, you take Jupiter on the meridian at dusk, bearing south. What is your latitude?
why: A planet on the meridian works like the Sun: z = 18°06.5′, south of you, so Lat = Dec + z = 17°08.4′ + 18°06.5′ = 35°14.9′N.

fig.title: Jupiter at dusk, 3 May 2027
lines: Jupiter on the meridian, bearing south

q: On the long leg to the Marquesas, Canopus crosses your meridian in evening twilight, bearing south. Where are you?

fig.title: Evening twilight, 15 Mar 2027
lines: Canopus on the meridian, bearing south

q: Between the Azores and Lisbon at morning twilight, you take Kochab on the meridian below the pole. What is your latitude?
why: Below the pole Lat = Ho + polar distance: 22°15.5′ + (90° − 74°04.0′ = 15°56.0′) = 38°11.5′N.

fig.title: Morning twilight, 25 Aug 2027
lines: Kochab at lower transit, bearing north

q: Leaving Newport, Rhode Island, for the Azores, you want a star to take below the pole at twilight. Which of these is circumpolar at your latitude?
why: Circumpolar when Dec exceeds the co-latitude, 90° − 41°30′ = 48°30′: only Dubhe (N61°38′) stays above the horizon below the pole.

q: Bound from the BVI to Bermuda, you take Polaris at evening twilight. What is your latitude?
At morning twilight on the ARC route you take Polaris. With which LHA Aries do you enter the a0 table?
why: LHA = GHA − west longitude: 171°44.8′ − 22°14′ = 149°30.8′. a0 comes from LHA Aries, a1 from latitude, a2 from the month.

q: At dusk you want Polaris, but it is faint and the sky is still bright. How do you find it in the sextant?
a: Set your DR latitude on the sextant and sweep the horizon due north
o: Wait for full darkness, when it is the brightest star in the north
Bring it down from overhead, as you would a bright star
Take the brightest star low in the north and use that
why: Polaris is only magnitude 2: preset its altitude (about your latitude), look due north, and it shows near the horizon in the scope.

q: On the leg from Panama to the Galápagos, a crew member suggests a Polaris sight for latitude. What do you decide?
a: Not worth it — a low, hazy sight with large refraction
o: Take it — Polaris gives latitude anywhere north of the equator
Take it, and add the refraction instead of subtracting it
Take it — at low latitude a0, a1 and a2 are all zero
why: Below about 10° refraction is large and uncertain and the horizon poor: use the noon Sun or a star well up for latitude.

fig.title: Polaris, DR 4°10′N 084°W
lines: Haze low on the northern horizon

q: In the South Pacific you find the south celestial pole by eye from the Southern Cross and the Pointers. What does its altitude give you?
a: A rough check on your south latitude, not a fix
o: Your latitude to the minute, as Polaris does in the north
Your longitude, if you note the time of the sight
Your south latitude, after the a0, a1 and a2 corrections
why: The pole's altitude equals your latitude, but with no bright star on it an estimate by eye can be a degree or more out.

q: On your plotting sheet you have run the morning sun line up to noon and drawn the noon latitude. Which point is your noon position?
why: The noon fix is where the run-up morning line (blue) cuts the noon latitude: A. B uses the line before it was run up.

q: You want a noon position from this morning's sun line. How do you bring the morning line up to noon?
a: Move it 18.4 M along 250°, keeping its direction
o: Move it 18.4 M along the Sun's azimuth, 118°
Turn it east–west to lie like the noon line
why: A position line is transferred by the run between the sights — course and distance made good — and keeps its direction.

q: You are running down the latitude of Hiva Oa on the Puddle Jump, and today's noon sight puts you here. What do you do?
a: Make good 12 M to the south
o: Make good 12 M to the north
Make good 6 M to the south
Make good 24 M to the south
why: In the south 9°48′S is 12′ further from the equator than 9°36′S: 12′ of latitude is 12 M to make good to the south.

fig.title: Noon, latitude sailing
lines: About 400 M still to the west

q: You have reached the latitude of Bridgetown, Barbados, and are running down it to the west. How far have you still to go?
why: Departure = DLo × cos lat = 151′ × cos 13°06′ = 147 M along the parallel.

q: Later in the day you find you never applied the index error to your noon sight. How does that move your noon latitude?
why: On the arc is subtracted, so your Ho was 2.4′ high and z 2.4′ small: Lat = Dec + z came out 2.4′ too far south.

q: On the ARC route you want a star on the meridian for a latitude at dusk. Which of these can you take?
a: Fomalhaut — between civil and nautical twilight
o: Altair — the brightest and highest of them
Enif — as soon as it crosses the meridian
Alpheratz — in full darkness, stars are sharpest
why: A star sight needs both the star and the horizon: only Fomalhaut crosses the meridian between 1750 and 1817.

q: Bound from the Galápagos to the Marquesas, a crew member suggests a Polaris sight for latitude tonight. What do you tell them?
a: It is below the horizon south of the equator
o: Fine — it gives latitude anywhere on Earth
Fine, but add the 1° instead of subtracting it
Only at midnight, when it is highest
why: Polaris' altitude is about your north latitude: in south latitudes it is below the horizon.

q: On a clear night north of the Azores you look for Polaris. Which star is it?
why: Follow the Plough's pointers, Merak to Dubhe, about five times their gap: Polaris sits alone in a dim patch of sky.

q: On a night watch in the South Pacific you look for the south celestial pole. Which point is it?
why: Extend the Cross's long axis, Gacrux to Acrux, about 4½ times its length; the Pointers' perpendicular bisector meets it there.

q: A new crew member asks why a single Polaris sight gives you your latitude. What do you tell them?
a: It sits within 1° of the pole, whose altitude equals your latitude
o: It is always on your meridian, like the Sun at noon
Its declination equals your latitude every night
Its altitude depends only on the date, as in the almanac
why: The celestial pole's altitude equals your latitude; Polaris is within 1° of it, and a0, a1, a2 correct for the difference.

q: You are making for Barbados across the Atlantic without GPS, by latitude sailing. Where do you plan to reach the island's latitude?
a: Well east of it, then run down the latitude to the west
o: Right at the island, on the great circle
A little north of it, then search either way
Well west of it, then work back to the east
why: Reach the latitude well up-wind and up-stream of the island: it is then dead ahead, and noon sights keep you on the parallel.

q: You are at 12°N in the southern Caribbean in mid-June. Where will you see the Sun at noon?
why: Dec N23°20′ is north of your 12°10′N, so at noon the Sun bears north: altitude 90° − (23°20′ − 12°10′) ≈ 79°.

q: Low cloud hides the Plough, but Cassiopeia's W is clear high in the north-east. Where do you look for Polaris?
a: About midway between Cassiopeia and the Plough
o: In the middle of Cassiopeia's W
On the far side of Cassiopeia from the Plough
At the end of the Plough's handle
why: Cassiopeia and the Plough lie on opposite sides of Polaris at about the same distance, so either one leads you to it.

q: Mid-Atlantic, your only watch has stopped and the GPS is dead. Which sight still gives you a reliable position line?
a: A noon latitude — it needs only the date's Dec
o: A morning sun line for longitude
A Sun and Moon fix by day
why: A meridian altitude needs no accurate time (Dec moves under 1′ an hour); every other sight needs UT to the second.

q: You cross the run-up morning sun line with your noon latitude, working by plane sailing. What is the longitude of your noon position?
why: Run the point 21.2 M on 260° → 15°19.4′N 41°25.5′W; down the line (219°) to 15°14.0′N is 4.4 M of westing → 41°30.0′W.

q: With the Sun nearly overhead, a crew member takes the noon sight at 1927 UT, four minutes early, and you work it as a meridian altitude. How far out is your latitude?
why: With the Sun 3° from the zenith the top is sharp: 4 min early it is 9′ low, so z is 9′ too big and Lat = Dec − z 9′ too far south.

q: Crossing from Cocos Keeling to Mauritius, you reduce this noon sight. What is your latitude?

fig.title: Noon sight, 15 Aug 2027
lines: IE 1.8′ off the arc, height of eye 2.5 m

q: Between Bermuda and the Azores you take Polaris at dusk. What is your latitude?
Bound from the Azores to Falmouth, you take Dubhe below the pole at morning twilight. What is your latitude?
South of the Azores you want Vega on the meridian at dusk. At what UT will it cross your meridian?
why: On the meridian LHA★ = 0, so GHA Aries = 25° − 80°33′ = 304°27′: 10°52.8′ past 2000 at 15°02.5′ an hour is 43 min → 2043 UT.

q: Mid-Pacific, just east of the date line, you work the noon sight for the ship's date. For which date and UT do you take the Sun's Dec?
why: 1210 LMT + 11h52m for 178°W = 2402 on 10 March, which is 0002 UT on 11 March: use the 11 March page.

q: At the spring equinox your noon latitude disagrees with the GPS, which has just come back. Which slip explains it?
a: Dec named N instead of S
o: SD for the upper limb used
why: The error is 59.8′ = 2 × 29.9′: Dec S was used as N. Dip added costs a few minutes, the wrong limb 32′, a late sight a fraction.

q: Your noon fix puts you north of Barbados' latitude. You want to reach 13°06′N 120 M to the west of you and then run down it. What true course do you steer?
why: Lose 14′ (14 M) of latitude over 120 M of departure: tan C = 14/120, 6.7° south of west → 263°.

q: On passage from Tonga to New Zealand you bring the Sun's upper limb down to the horizon at noon. What is your latitude?

fig.title: Noon sight, 10 Nov 2026
lines: IE 2.2′ on the arc, height of eye 2.8 m

q: Between Mauritius and the Seychelles you take the noon Sun by its upper limb. What Ho do you work your latitude from?
why: Hs 55°27.7′ + 1.4′ IE off the arc − 2.5′ dip − 0.7′ refraction − 15.7′ SD (upper limb) = Ho 55°10.2′.
ref: Meridian altitude — from Hs to Ho

fig.title: Noon sight, 20 Jul 2026
lines: IE 1.4′ off the arc, height of eye 2.0 m

q: Two days out of the Canaries for Cape Verde, you take the noon sight at 1325 UT. What is your latitude?

fig.title: Noon sight, 20 Oct 2026
lines: IE 1.6′ on the arc, height of eye 2.4 m

q: Bound from Fremantle to Mauritius, you took the noon Sun by its upper limb but worked it with the lower-limb correction. How does that move your latitude?
why: +SD instead of −SD makes Ho 2 × 16.3′ = 32.6′ too high; z is that much too small, and with the Sun north of you Lat = Dec − z comes out 32.6′ too far north.
ref: Meridian altitude — from Hs to Ho

fig.title: Noon, 12 Jan 2027
lines: Upper limb observed, Sun bearing north

q: At noon thin cloud covers the lower half of the Sun, but its upper edge is sharp against the sky. What do you do?
a: Bring the upper limb to the horizon and subtract the SD
o: Bring the centre to the horizon and apply no SD
Guess where the lower limb is and use that
Give up the noon sight until tomorrow
why: Use the limb you can see: the upper limb's correction subtracts the semi-diameter (about 16′) where the lower limb's adds it.
ref: Meridian altitude — from Hs to Ho

fig.title: Noon sight
lines: Thin cloud over the Sun's lower half

q: A day short of Rio on passage from Cape Town, you find the noon Sun will pass almost overhead. How do you get your latitude today?
a: Time sights either side of noon and plot each as a circle round the GP
o: Take the maximum as usual — a high Sun gives the best noon
Average the sights taken ten minutes either side of noon
Note the Sun's bearing at noon and take your latitude as the Dec
why: Within a degree of the zenith the bearing swings fast and the peak is hard to catch: each timed sight is a small circle, radius z, round the GP.
ref: Meridian altitude — Sun near the zenith

q: Bound from Tahiti to Hawaii, you plot a sight taken four minutes after noon as a circle round the Sun's GP. What radius do you draw?
why: Radius = zenith distance: 90° − 87°50.0′ = 2°10.0′ = 130 minutes of arc = 130.0 M, centred on the GP.
ref: Meridian altitude — Sun near the zenith

q: South of Bermuda, bound for the Virgin Islands, the crew hand you this noon altitude but cannot say which way they faced. Which latitude can it give?
o: 18°04.5′N only — in May the Sun bears north
why: z = 90° − 88°41.6′ = 1°18.4′: Sun north gives Dec − z = 18°04.5′N, Sun south Dec + z = 20°41.3′N. Only the bearing or a good DR decides.
ref: Meridian altitude — Sun near the zenith

q: You are delivering a motor yacht from Newport to Bermuda at 24 knots, heading south towards the noon Sun. When will the sextant show the greatest altitude?
a: A few minutes after LAN — you are closing the Sun
o: A few minutes before LAN — your speed brings noon forward
At LAN exactly — the boat's speed makes no difference
At 1200 ship's time, whatever the longitude
why: Running towards the Sun adds about 24′ of altitude an hour, so it keeps rising after LAN: the peak comes late, and a little too high.

q: Bound north from Bermuda to Newport at 25 knots, you follow the Sun up at noon. When will you see its greatest altitude?
o: At LAN, as on any boat
why: Running away from the Sun costs 25′/h = 0.42′ a minute; the curve falls 0.030′ × t², so the top comes 0.42 ÷ (2 × 0.030) ≈ 7 min early.

fig.title: Motor yacht, 20 Nov 2026
lines: Near LAN the altitude falls 0.030′ × t²

q: On a fast motor yacht running north or south, how do you get a true meridian altitude at noon?
a: Take the altitude at the predicted time of LAN by the watch
o: Take the maximum, as on any boat — it always falls at LAN
Take the maximum and add your speed in minutes of arc
Take the sight ten minutes after LAN, when it settles
why: A fast north–south run shifts the peak off the meridian: take the sight at the computed LAN by the watch, or slow down for it.

q: Between Bermuda and the Azores in June, the first-quarter Moon crosses your meridian at dusk, bearing south. What is your latitude?

fig.title: Moon at dusk, June
lines: Moon (LL) on the meridian, bearing south

q: In the Marquesas you want the Moon on your meridian tonight. At what UT will it cross?
why: The Moon is 49 min later each day: 1752 + 49 × 140/360 = 1811 LMT at 140°W; + 9h20m = 2731, i.e. 0331 UT on 15 July.

q: Crossing from Mauritius to Durban in late February, you catch Venus on the meridian in the afternoon sky, bearing north. What is your latitude?

fig.title: Venus by day
lines: Venus on the meridian, bearing north

q: You take Jupiter on the meridian at dusk. From which Ho do you work your latitude?
why: A planet takes IE, dip and refraction only: 44°36.2′ − 1.2′ − 2.8′ − 1.0′ = 44°31.2′. No semi-diameter: it is a point of light.

q: You took the Moon on the meridian at 0352 UT but worked it with the Dec for 03h. How far out is your latitude?
why: The Moon's Dec moves 13.5′ an hour: 52 minutes is 11.7′. The Dec you used is that much too far south, and so is your latitude.

q: Hove-to for a day in a winter gale south of the Azores, with no almanac to hand, you take Kochab at both its transits. What is your latitude?
why: Above and below the pole the star is the same distance from it, so Lat = (50°14.4′ + 18°22.4′) ÷ 2 = 34°18.4′N, with no Dec needed.

q: Approaching Svalbard at midsummer, you have lost the almanac overboard. You take the Sun at noon, bearing south, and at midnight, bearing north. What is your latitude?
why: The Sun crosses on both sides of the zenith: Lat = 90° − (36°12.5′ − 10°35.9′) ÷ 2 = 77°11.7′N. The mean, 23°24.2′, is its Dec.

q: North of Norway in July, a crew member plans a Polaris sight for tonight's latitude. What do you tell them?
a: No darkness, no Polaris — take the midnight Sun bearing north
o: Take it at local midnight, the darkest moment
Take it — at 76°N it is nearly overhead, so z is tiny
Take it, but this far north skip a0, a1 and a2
why: At 76°N in July the Sun stays about 8° up at midnight: no stars. Its lower transit gives latitude: Lat = Ho + (90° − Dec).

fig.title: Barents Sea, 10 Jul 2027
lines: Sun at local midnight: 8° up, bearing north

q: On the southern route from Cape Verde to Grenada, you take Polaris low in the north at dusk. What is your latitude?
You have taken Polaris near 10°N and, on another passage, near 50°N. What is true of the low sight?
a: Its refraction is larger and less certain — the horizon needs care
o: Its a0 correction is larger, as the star circles wider
It gives you longitude as well as latitude
It needs no dip correction, being so low
why: a0 depends on LHA Aries, not on latitude. Polaris 10° up carries about 5′ of refraction, which haze and temperature can upset.

fig.title: Two Polaris sights
lines: Same sextant, same height of eye

q: Bound from Oman to India in January, you take Polaris at dusk. With which LHA Aries do you enter the a0 table?
why: LHA = GHA + east longitude: 317°21.7′ + 64°30′ = 381°51.7′; take off 360° to enter the table at 21°51.7′.

q: At dusk on the ARC route you take Polaris. What is your latitude?
Sailing the South Atlantic, a new crew member asks how you will get a latitude at dusk with no pole star. What do you tell them?
a: A bright star's meridian altitude, such as Achernar or Canopus
o: The south celestial pole's altitude, corrected by a0
Polaris, low on the northern horizon
The Southern Cross's altitude at any time
why: No bright star marks the south pole: take a bright star as it crosses your meridian in twilight and use Lat = Dec ± z.

q: Between Rodrigues and Mauritius at dusk just after Christmas, Achernar crosses your meridian, bearing south. What is your latitude?

fig.title: Evening twilight, 28 Dec 2026
lines: Achernar on the meridian, bearing south

q: Crossing the Tasman from Hobart to New Zealand in early December, you take Acrux below the south pole at dusk. What is your latitude?
why: Below the pole Lat = Ho + polar distance: 14°22.5′ + (90° − 63°14.0′ = 26°46.0′) = 41°08.5′, named like the pole: S.

fig.title: Evening twilight, 1 Dec 2026
lines: Acrux at lower transit, bearing south

q: At evening twilight in the Indian Ocean you see the Southern Cross standing upright like this. What does it tell you?
a: Acrux is on your meridian — time for its meridian altitude
o: The Cross is due east — a good star for longitude
Acrux is at its lowest, at lower transit
The Cross is setting — too low to use
why: With Gacrux straight above Acrux the long axis is vertical: the Cross is at upper transit, bearing south, on your meridian.

q: Your crew points out a cross of stars, larger and dimmer than you expected, with no bright pair beside it. What is it most likely to be?
a: The False Cross — the true one is smaller, with the Pointers by it
o: The Southern Cross, looking larger near the horizon
The Southern Cross upside down, at lower transit
The Northern Cross, seen from the south
why: The False Cross (in Carina and Vela) is bigger and fainter; the real Cross is compact, with α and β Centauri pointing to it.

q: A crew member asks for the 'southern Polaris' to take for latitude tonight. What do you tell them?
a: There is none to use — Sigma Octantis is too faint
o: Acrux — it sits on the south pole
Canopus — work it with the a0 tables
Achernar — it never moves in the sky
why: Sigma Octantis, about 1° from the south pole, is only magnitude 5.4, too faint for a sextant. Use a bright star's meridian altitude.

q: Two days out of Fremantle for Mauritius, at 30°S, you want a star to take below the south pole at twilight. Which of these stays above your horizon all night?
why: Circumpolar when the Dec exceeds the co-latitude, 90° − 30° = 60°: only Acrux (S63°14′) stays up; Achernar (S57°06′) just sets.

q: Running down the latitude of Antigua, you find the noon sights creeping north. Which course now keeps you on the latitude?
why: A set of 7 M a day to the north is 0.29 kn; at 6.5 kn that needs asin(0.29/6.5) ≈ 3°: steer 3° south of west, 267°.

fig.title: Latitude sailing to Antigua
lines: Back on 17°00′N today after a correction

q: Bound for Bermuda from the Azores, your noon fix puts you north of the latitude you want, with a current setting north. What course do you steer?
why: The track to the target is 261° (25 M south in 150 M west); to cancel 0.5 kn of set to the north at 6 kn, steer about 5° further south: 256°.

fig.note: Current 000° 0.5 kn · speed 6 kn · not to scale

q: On the run from the Marquesas to the Tuamotus, today's noon latitude differs from your DR. What does it tell you about the current?
o: Nothing — a latitude cannot show current
why: 13′ south of the DR after 24 h of good steering and log: 13 M ÷ 24 h ≈ 0.5 kn of southerly set. The east–west part stays unknown.

fig.title: Noon, 24 h after the last fix

q: Running down the latitude of Ascension with no good longitude, at noon you have the island 60 M ahead by DR, give or take 25 M. What is your plan?
a: Slow down and close the island at first light
o: Hold 6 kn — its light will show you at night
Speed up to arrive before dark
Alter 30° north to be sure of passing clear
why: With 25 M of doubt you could arrive any time from dusk to the small hours: slow down, keep to the latitude, close the island in daylight.

fig.title: Noon, latitude sailing
lines: On 7°56′S, Ascension 60 M ahead by DR

q: You advance your noon latitude to dusk and cross it with this star line. What is the longitude of the fix?
why: Noon lat run 39 M on 225° → 23°42.4′N; intercept point 23°58.4′N 45°26.3′W; along 165° to 23°42.4′N is 4.3 M east → 45°21.6′W.

q: At dusk on the ARC route you want one star to cross with your noon latitude, run up to the time of the sight. Which do you choose?
why: A latitude runs east–west, so the best cut comes from a star bearing near east or west: Altair at 256° crosses it at 76°.

q: Two days out of Cape Town for St Helena, you advance your noon latitude to dusk for a star fix. Where does the advanced latitude lie?
why: A latitude line moves only by the run's change of latitude: 36.0 M × cos 315° = 25.5′ north, so 25°42.0′S becomes 25°16.5′S.

q: Cloud hides the Sun from mid-morning until 1530, when it comes out. You have a 0900 sun line. How do you get a fix?
a: Run the 0900 line up to 1530 and cross it with a 1530 sun line
o: Work the 1530 sight as a late meridian altitude
Cross the 0900 and 1530 lines without running up
Wait for tomorrow's noon — one sun line is worthless
why: Sun–run–sun: transfer the morning line by the run and cross it with the afternoon line; the Sun's bearing has swung 135°.

q: Bound from Bermuda to Antigua, with cloud closing in, you take the Sun six minutes before noon and reduce it as an ex-meridian. What is your latitude?
Cloud hid the Sun at its peak, but you caught the same sextant altitude before and after noon. What is your longitude?
why: LAN is midway, 2025:45½ UT. The Sun crosses Greenwich at 1144:45, so 8h41m00½s × 15 = 130°15.1′ of west longitude.

q: Leaving Fiji for Vanuatu, the ship's clock still on Fiji time (zone −12), you plan the noon sight at 177°30′E. When, in UT, is the Sun on your meridian?
why: 1209 LMT − 11h50m for 177°30′E = 0019 UT on the same date, 15 January: east longitude is subtracted, and no day is crossed.

q: On the ARC route the crew took today's noon sight standing on the coachroof, but you reduced it for your usual cockpit height. How does that move your latitude?
why: Dip for 3.5 m is 3.3′, for 2.0 m 2.5′: Ho came out 0.8′ too high and z too small, so with the Sun south Lat = Dec + z is 0.8′ too far south.
ref: Meridian altitude — from Hs to Ho

lines: Sun bearing south, you in north latitude

q: A new watchkeeper offers to take the noon sight 'at 1200 by the ship's clock'. What do you tell them?
a: Noon is when the Sun crosses our meridian — from Mer Pass and longitude
o: Fine — the ship's clock is set to local noon
Fine, as long as the clock is checked against UT
Take it at 1200 UT, the almanac's noon
why: Local noon is the Sun's meridian passage: Mer Pass in LMT plus or minus your longitude in time — rarely 1200 on any clock.

q: On the South Atlantic crossing from Cape Town to Brazil in July, a crew member used to the Med starts the noon sight facing south. Where should they look?
why: Dec N21° is north of your 30°S, so the noon Sun bears north at 90° − (30° + 21°) = 39°.

q: Jupiter crosses your meridian at 0130 local time, high and brilliant in a moonless sky. Do you take it for latitude?
a: No — there is no horizon to bring it down to
o: Yes — a planet is bright enough at any hour
Yes, and add 15′ for the dark horizon
Only if it bears north of you
why: A sextant sight needs a sharp horizon: stars and planets are taken in twilight, when both the body and the horizon can be seen.

q: A day out of Cape Town in mid-April, you preset the sextant before noon so the Sun is ready in the telescope. What do you set, and where do you look?
why: Dec N11°20′ and your 33°40′S are on opposite sides of the equator: z = 33°40′ + 11°20′ = 45°, so the Sun is about 45° up, to the north.

q: Overcast all day has cost you the noon sight, but the sky is clearing from the west at dusk. What is the next best latitude tonight?
a: A star on the meridian, or Polaris, in evening twilight
o: The Moon at midnight, whatever the horizon
Tomorrow's noon — no other sight gives latitude
A star low in the east, as soon as it rises
why: Any body on your meridian gives latitude, and Polaris does at any hour in the north — in twilight, with a sharp horizon.

lines: Clearing from the west at dusk

q: You plan to take the Moon on the meridian. Which almanac figure do you need that you never use for the Sun?
why: The Moon is so close that its parallax reaches a degree: parallax in altitude = HP × cos Ha. The Sun's is only about 0.1′.

q: At dusk in early March you take Capella and Rigel on the meridian minutes apart, and the two latitudes disagree. Which do you plot?
why: An error common to both sights (IE, dip) moves a north star's latitude one way and a south star's the other: their mean cancels it.

q: After plotting your noon fix from the run-up morning line, you find the noon latitude was 4.0′ too far north. How does the fix move?
why: The fix slides along the run-up line (030°–210°): 4.0′ of latitude south along it is 4.0 ÷ cos 30° = 4.6 M towards 210°.
